canberra.title: Aquatic centre must not be collateral damage in new stadium push, say pool supporters
canberra.snippet: A proposal for a new stadium at Regatta Place should not swamp plans for the Canberra Aquatic Centre in Commonwealth Park, pool supporter...
canberra.content:
A concept illustration of the Canberra Aquatic Centre, sitting to the south of the church land. Image: NCA.

A proposal for a new stadium at Regatta Place should not swamp plans for the Canberra Aquatic Centre in Commonwealth Park, pool supporters say.

Friends of Canberra Olympic Pool president Terry Slevin said the proposal from a Canberra Airport led consortium had sent a ripple of anxiety through Canberra’s aquatic community.

Mr Slevin said the proponents had not paid much attention to the aquatic centre proposal, which has land and $138 million already allocated to it.

“I understand the excitement of the access to the land around the Archbishop’s House. I’m very conscious of the constraint that provided even on the planning for the aquatic centre,” he said.

“So I understand the excitement of taking the best possible advantage of that prime location but as part of the mix, I don’t want to see the interests of the people who use a pool 363 days a year kicked into the long grass.”

Mr Slevin said whether the two facilities could sit side by side was a technical question that only Infrastructure Canberra could answer.

He did not have a clear sense of the precise footprint of the Archbishop’s House and land and whether it was viable to put the two together.

There were examples of pools attached to stadiums such as the Sydney Football Stadium development in Moore Park, but that was a 25-metre pool not a 10-lane Olympic facility where regional competitions could happen.

“Ideally we’d have a dive pool which is under cover and usable 12 months of the year,” Mr Slevin said.

“That’s a cost consideration in the development of the aquatic centre at the moment, and those are things that are still up in the air.

“But what’s viable in the combined available land parcel and taking into account environmental considerations and the other infrastructure that exists there, that’s a technical question.”

Canberra Olympic Pool should not close until there is an alternative, says pool lobby. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Mr Slevin said he would be happy to sit down with airport boss Stephen Byron to discuss the situation.

As someone involved in the conference industry, a Brumbies fan and a swimmer, he had a personal investment in Canberra having a decent convention centre, a new stadium to replace the ageing Bruce facility and an adequate aquatic centre when the Canberra Olympic Pool makes way for the planned Convention and Entertainment Centre.

“The real question is how can this happen in a practical manner and particularly given that we’ve already had a financial commitment [to the pool] since 2024 and the planning process has started,” Mr Slevin said.

“We’re two years down the track and there hasn’t been a contract yet for anybody building a new aquatic facility or even putting forward a very specific design.

“I wouldn’t be rushing to buy the tickets for the Raiders or the Brumbies for winter 2030 at Civic just yet.”

Mr Slevin said unpicking the land tenure and planning work for the pool, if it came to that, and changing the lease for Archbishop’s House would not happen overnight.

Mr Slevin hoped a new convention centre, a new stadium, and a new pool could be achieved but government would need to fund it and money was tight.

“Ultimately those things come down to an expression of priority, and so we’ll be making a loud noise to make sure that the pool remains a high priority,” he said.

Mr Slevin agreed that the proposal and what it would bring to the area was attractive but “it’s about what you can fit in and what you can afford”.

“And also don’t forget that Floriade’s still running and there’s a very big interest in ensuring that the footprint of Floriade is protected,” he said.

“We’ve got 48 hours so far and a whole lot more thinking and a lot of tape measures need to be pulled out of the back pocket and run over bits of land to figure out what’s possible.”

Mr Slevin’s members were clear that the existing pool should not close until there was an alternative.

The Archdiocese of Canberra and Goulburn said no decision had been made to sell the property.

“We were approached about a proposal involving the site and have agreed to participate in preliminary discussions,” a spokesperson said.

“As a longstanding part of the Canberra community, we are always willing to be involved in discussions about the future flourishing of the national capital and the communities which make up its rich tapestry.

The spokesperson said discussions were at a very early stage, and Archbishop’s House continued to be used.

“The Archdiocese is open to hearing and considering the proposal, but no decision has been made about the future of the property,” the spokesperson said.

canberra.title: Chalmers forces ATO to delay its credit card ban, while Greens say banks should wear card surcharge
canberra.snippet: The Australian Taxation Office has been forced to delay its ban on accepting credit card payments for another six months, following an ou...
canberra.content:
The Federal Government should force banks to carry the costs of credit card transactions instead of passing them on to small business, say the Greens. Photo: File.

The Australian Taxation Office has been forced to delay its ban on accepting credit card payments for another six months, following an outcry from the business sector, which has to absorb card payment surcharges or increase prices.

The ATO decided to refuse credit card payments from 1 December, saying it was not tenable for it to absorb the surcharges since the Federal Government’s ban came into effect this month.

But Treasurer Jim Chalmers has now stepped in to delay the ATO’s credit card ban until the new financial year.

“Australian small businesses have said the ATO’s announced timeframe was inadequate and we have taken these concerns seriously and acted on them,” he said on Friday (9 October) in a joint statement with Small Business Minister Anne Aly and Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino.

“The government will provide transitional funding so the ATO can continue accepting credit card transactions until the end of the financial year, with costs to be finalised in MYEFO.

“This will provide more time for the ATO to engage with small business and other taxpayers who currently rely on credit cards, provide more detailed information to those affected, and consult on targeted options to support impacted taxpayers.”

The Treasurer’s intervention follows days of mixed messages from government ministers over the ATO’s credit card ban.

Earlier on Friday, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said it was pretty clear the government could not force the ATO to reverse its decision to stop accepting credit card payments.

“They are independent. Governments can’t direct the tax office to implement tax in a certain way,” Senator Wong told Channel Nine.

“What we can do is say to them, you should be consulting with small business, and we would really encourage the ATO to engage with small business about this.

“I know that only a small proportion of small businesses were using credit cards for this, but obviously it is a change.”

Environment Minister Murray Watt told Channel Seven that “various ministers” were making their view known to the ATO and expressing the government’s expectations.

“We need to keep it in perspective, that when it comes to payments to the ATO, it’s only a very small number of taxpayers who pay their tax payments by credit card,” he said.

“It’s about 5 per cent for small businesses and about 2 per cent for individuals.

“We were very clear with the ATO when they first proposed this, that they needed to have a transition plan, that they needed to work properly with the business community.

“And I’m sure that those expectations will be reinforced.”

However, other government ministers had previously suggested there was little to no consultation over the ATO’s move.

Housing Minister Clare O’Neil said on Thursday that Labor had “real concerns” over the ATO’s move.

Ms Aly said something similar, but Assistant Minister for the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton backed the ATO decision.

Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume said Labor could force the ATO to back down “with the stroke of a pen” if it wanted to.

“You can’t blame the ATO. They’re your agency. You’re the government. You can do this,” Senator Hume said.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has described it as “open warfare” inside the government.

“Small businesses deserve better than eight hours’ notice, and a circus of ministers fumbling their lines and making up policy on the run,” he said.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry has repeatedly called for the Federal Government to step in.

“If the Australian Taxation Office can’t find its way out of the maze it has created, then it’s time for political leadership to step in and fix this,” CEO Andrew McKellar said.

Meanwhile, the Greens say the Federal Government should force banks to carry the costs of credit card surcharges themselves.

Greens deputy leader Steph Hodgins-May said the government could assist small businesses, who currently have to absorb the card surcharges or put up their prices, by putting the onus back onto banks.

She insists Labor should force the banking sector to absorb the costs of card transactions.

“Labor needs to put down rules that will protect business – small business who are already doing it incredibly tough at this point,” Senator Hodgins-May said.

“And also the greed of big banks – they need to regulate the banks.

“This falls back on Labor. It was as predictable, I’d say, as the sun rising.

“And they have a responsibility in the depths of a cost-of-living crisis to regulate the banks and ensure that this does not get pushed on to consumers and to small business.”

canberra.title: Chaos and confusion: Five taken to hospital after car crashes into business
canberra.snippet: UPDATE: Five people have been taken to hospital, two in a serious condition, after a car crashed into a Canberra business earlier today (...
canberra.content:
9 October 2026

A massage clinic was cordoned off in the aftermath of the incident. Photos: Ruby Garrety.

UPDATE: Five people have been taken to hospital, two in a serious condition, after a car crashed into a Canberra business earlier today (9 October) causing “chaos and confusion”.

At about 11:45 am, the car drove into a massage clinic on Trenerry St, near Cooleman Court, in Weston, trapping three people under the vehicle.

A person who was in the store at the time received minor injuries but was able to walk out.

Speaking this afternoon, ACT Ambulance Operations Manager Chris Tyrrell said five people were taken to Canberra Hospital.

He said it was “frankly outstanding that the injuries weren’t more severe”.

“The fact that we’re only dealing with lower limb injuries, albeit serious lower limb injuries, is quite fortunate,“ Mr Tyrrell said.

Two people were in a serious but stable condition, while another two had minor injuries. The fifth person was in a stable condition.

ACT Fire and Rescue Commander Jeff Dau said emergency services arrived to a “scene of chaos and confusion”.

It took them about 45 minutes to extricate the three people from under the car.

“We used airbags to raise the vehicle, and with that we were able to release the entrapped patients,” he said.

He said the building itself appeared structurally stable.

ACT Policing Detective Sergeant Jonathan Turkich alleged the driver was an 84-year-old woman.

He said she had tested negative for drugs and alcohol, and was assisting police.

“There’s no suggestion to me that this is any sort of deliberate action, so people can be calm about that,” he said.

He also called for anyone with dashcam footage of the incident to come forward.

Detective Sergeant Turkich said the incident was a reminder for Canberrans to think of each other.

“Our hearts go out to the victims, go out to the wider community impacted by this, because as you can see from the response and the people around [here], it affects everyone.”

Photos: Ruby Garrety.

Photos: Ruby Garrety.

Photos: Ruby Garrety.

Photos: Ruby Garrety.

Photos: Ruby Garrety.

1 PM: Four people were left trapped under a car near Cooleman Court after a car drove into a shopfront today (Friday, 9 October).

An ACT Policing spokesperson confirmed that multiple emergency services were on the scene of a massage clinic on Trenerry Street in Weston around 12 pm.

An ACT Emergency Services Agency (ACT ESA) spokesperson said that a car appeared to have lost control before driving into a shopfront.

“This has resulted in four people being stuck under a car for some time,” they said.

Several people were taken to hospital this afternoon, but police could not provide information on their condition.

The driver has also been taken to hospital with minor injuries.

canberra.title: Wagga foodie tour: Moroccan pancakes, sticky pork taco and Wagyu skirt
canberra.snippet: If you’re in Canberra and fancy a foodie weekend away, you don’t necessarily need to head to Sydney or Melbourne. Wagga is about a 2.5-ho...
canberra.content:
I tried to pour the tea like Mustapha and ended up with third-degree burns. Photos: Oliver Jacques.

If you’re in Canberra and fancy a foodie weekend away, you don’t necessarily need to head to Sydney or Melbourne.

Wagga is about a 2.5-hour drive away – and I reckon it’s got more than enough good food to justify making the trip.

Riverina may have a reputation as Australia’s fast-food capital, but scratch beneath that and you’ll find seriously good restaurants, from Moroccan and Thai to modern Australian and some very good steaks.

Best of all, you can actually enjoy your weekend. No spending half the day stuck in traffic, circling for a parking spot or queuing for a table.

I recently had what I reckon was the perfect Wagga foodie Saturday, and if you’re a Canberra food lover looking for an easy weekend escape, here’s a lead you can follow.

Breakfast at Al Maghrib

A colourful full Moroccan breakfast.

First stop was Al Maghrib on Fitzmaurice Street, which I believe is the only Moroccan restaurant in regional NSW.

Owner Mustapha El Mourtazak is one of those welcoming chefs who make a restaurant feel like a restaurant. He’ll charm you while pouring Moroccan mint tea from what seems like an impossible distance, and his enthusiasm for his food and culture is infectious.

I went for the Moroccan pancakes, known as msemmen.

They’re nothing like the fluffy pancakes you might expect at an Australian cafe. They’re thin, flaky and layered, with a slightly crisp, golden exterior and a buttery, almost pastry-like texture inside. I had it alongside a spicy omelette served in a clay pot.

Al Maghrib describes itself as a contemporary Moroccan cafe, with traditional dishes including shakshuka and tagines.

And the best part is that you don’t need to take out a second mortgage to eat there.

Lunch at Mr Lawrence

The sticky pork taco doesn’t look like the tacos I’m used to.

I barely digested breakfast before I was back at it.

Mr Lawrence, also on Fitzmaurice Street, is one of those places that makes it difficult to order sensibly.

It describes itself as somewhere between a cafe, restaurant and bar, and its menu moves comfortably between breakfast classics, lunch dishes, cocktails and more adventurous combinations.

I went for the sticky pork taco, served on pan-fried roti rather than a traditional taco shell, with kimchi, coriander, shallot, sesame and sweet fish sauce.

The result is a terrific combination of sweet, salty, spicy and fresh, with the crisp-edged roti giving it far more character than your standard taco.

I also shared the ginger and prawn dumplings, served with tamari, chilli and fried shallots.

They were a good little preview of what is coming next from owner Jamie Shepley, who is about to open Wagga’s first Asian fusion restaurant, Madamelle, upstairs.

Dinner at Hide Steak & Bar

Check out the caramelisation on the steak.

By dinner I was ready for the main event. Steak.

I’ve lived in Sydney and Buenos Aires and eaten at some of the great steakhouses around the world.

I reckon Hide is the best. That might sound like a big call for a Wagga restaurant, but I stand by it.

Chef Sârn Rudd and her husband Darren now own Hide; they took over from Jamie Shepley and have continued to build the restaurant around Australian beef and locally grown produce.

The restaurant now operates from Morgan Street and cooks over local mallee charcoal, with a dry-ageing program designed to develop more flavour, tenderness and character in the beef.

We started with lamb cutlets, served with Wagga Black Garlic, and homemade focaccia. Both superb.

The Black Angus scotch fillet I ordered for a main had great caramelisation – a dark, salty, almost burnt crust giving way to beautifully tender beef underneath.

My wife Jenna ordered the Wagyu inside skirt. I spent quite a bit of the evening trying to steal it – it was beautifully tender and practically melted in the mouth.

But perhaps the best thing about Hide is that the staff know the menu backwards. Tell them what sort of meat you like, how hungry you are and what you’re drinking, and they can steer you towards the right cut and a wine to go with it. That makes a big difference.

The verdict

Didn’t think Wagga was a foodie haven? Think again.

We’re blessed with some seriously good food in the Riverina – and it’s not just Wagga. Albury, Griffith, Leeton, Narrandera and Junee can all hold their own.

I also love Larry’s, Meccanico Espresso + Wine Bar, Nabiha’s Kitchen, Banh Mi 88 and Thaigga, and there are plenty more I haven’t even got to yet.

Wagga might have mastered the drive-through, but it has also quietly built a food scene that’s well worth the drive.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: Massive rate hike or service cuts? Yass Valley Council weighs options for $8.3m shortfall
canberra.snippet: Yass residents would face a cumulative rate hike of up to 76.55 per cent if its local council were to rely solely on rates to fix a more ...
canberra.content:
9 October 2026

Join the conversation

2

Financial modelling suggests Yass residents could face big rate hikes. Photo: Yass Valley Council.

Yass residents would face a cumulative rate hike of up to 76.55 per cent if its local council were to rely solely on rates to fix a more than $8 million budget hole.

AEC Group was engaged to review Yass Valley Council’s (YVC) financial situation.

Its report found the council needs $8.3 million a year by 2027/28 to maintain its position.

AEC Group’s Graham Jarvis told a council-organised community forum that while YVC had improved its budget, further action was needed.

“That needs to be corrected in terms of the cash generated from operations,” he said of the $8 million figure.

“You can either do that through increasing revenue, or you can do it through decreasing expenditure, or a combination of both. But the fix is $8.3 million dollars a year.”

He said costs associated with YVC’s general fund had grown at 8.45 per cent over seven years, while income from YVC’s general fund had only increased by about 5 per cent.

He also said the council is currently paying interest on loans taken out for the Crago Mill project.

“But once that requires you to pay interest and borrowings, it’s a $3 million commitment a year,” he said.

“Council, an additional $3 million a year in itself is 20 per cent of your rate base.”

He also said a “broad spend” on infrastructure maintenance was also needed, describing this as a “long-term burn”.

Mr Jarvis told the forum that if YVC wanted to rely on people’s rates to solve its financial problems, it would need a cumulative rate hike of up to 76.55 per cent.

The council has not yet decided whether to apply for a special rate variation (SRV), or what a potential increase may be.

For an increase to go ahead, YVC would need to make a formal application to the Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal.

In late 2025, when it considered proposals to hike rates by between 40 and 58.70 per cent, councillors deferred a decision to 2026.

Mr Jarvis also said that service changes could be utilised to help cover the council’s budget.

“You could deliver the service in a different way, and yet still provide the same level of service,” he said.

Depending on the approach, this could include outsourcing, sharing service delivery with another council, changing how YVC staff schedule their shifts, or buying things at a lower cost.

The meeting heard that YVC roads and contractors were at the top of the list of where council’s money was being spent.

In a statement after the forum, YVC CEO Gayleen Burley said the independent review was confronting.

“Council has already made operational savings and improved efficiencies and that work will continue.

“But the independent analysis tells us that these steps alone will not close the gap while addressing our infrastructure needs, maintaining services and meeting our debt commitments.”

Councillors will consider a response at an upcoming public forum and extraordinary meeting on 14 October from 4 pm.

This will be livestreamed through the council’s YouTube page, while agenda information is available on YVC’s website.

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

australia.title: New spate of stabbings, overdoses and fires at Australian immigration detention centres run by ICE-linked US prison firm
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Federal government under scrutiny as documents reveal serious security lapses at Melbourne and Villawood immigration detention...
australia.content:
A new spate of stabbings, overdoses and drug use in Australia’s immigration detention centres has put the Australian government in likely breach of laws designed to protect staff and detainees, internal documents show.

Earlier this year, Guardian Australia revealed catastrophic security failings across Australia’s onshore immigration network since Management and Training Corporation – a US private prison company used by Donald Trump to hold ICE detainees – won the $2.3bn detention contract in late 2024.

The federal government has repeatedly attempted to take a stick to MTC and its local subsidiary Secure Journeys to improve its performance, including through financial penalties and a fiery meeting last year between the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, and the company’s global president.

But new documents seen by the Guardian show serious security lapses have continued since, including through a spate of eight fire-related incidents at Villawood immigration detention centre and violence and drug use at Melbourne immigration detention centre (MIDC). Those failings have again put the department itself in the crosshairs of Comcare, the federal work safety regulator.

The documents reveal a string of incidents at MIDC involving violence, aggression, illicit substances and improvised weaponry since August. That includes a violent altercation on 18 August between two groups that led to six detainees being hospitalised for “slashing and stabbing injuries made using improvised weapons”.

On 10 September, a detainee was found overdosed in his room, requiring staff to administer Naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdose effects.

The incidents at MIDC prompted Comcare to warn the government that it was failing to control the rising number of “incidents of this type at MIDC and across the broader immigration detention network”. That failure meant it was likely to be in breach of the law, the document said.

“I have formed the reasonable belief that the department is contravening section 19 of the WHS Act by failing to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and other persons,” Comcare said in its notice. “In particular, the risks associated with violence, aggression, and the presence of illicit substances and improvised weaponry are not being adequately managed.

“While the department has advised that a range of actions have been undertaken to address these risks, it has not sufficiently demonstrated that the control measures currently in place are effective in eliminating or minimising the risks, so far as is reasonably practicable.”

Comcare said the information available indicates these hazards pose an ongoing risk of serious harm to workers and others in the centres.

A separate Comcare document revealed that a series of eight fire-related incidents had taken place at Villawood immigration detention centre between February and May.

That’s despite prior warnings to government to intervene after previous fires lit inside Villawood exposed serious gaps in MTC’s preparedness. That includes one fire on 23 September 2025, when MTC staff rushed into a detainee’s room to save him from a fire without proper safety equipment, causing two workers to be hospitalised.

The regulator found the department had not conducted its own systematic review of “all fire and smoke control measures falling within its influence or control”, a likely breach of work health and safety regulations.

“The occurrence of multiple notifiable fire incidents over a period of approximately four months, particularly after previous regulatory intervention concerning substantially the same risk, provided repeated and compelling circumstances requiring the department to review the effectiveness of relevant control measures,” the Comcare document said.

The Guardian previously revealed a series of incidents across the centres since Secure Journey took over, including escapes, staff injuries and sick detainees missing medical appointments due to a lack of staff to escort them.

Lyndal Ryan, national president of the United Workers Union, which represents workers in the centres, said the notices from Comcare show “the continuing dangerous situations facing workers and detainees inside detention centres, and Secure Journeys’ inability or unwillingness to address those issues”.

The union has continually raised concerns about understaffing in the centres, and Ryan said Comcare has made it clear that the department has the responsibility to pull Secure Journeys into line.

“The list of eight fires at Villawood over a four-month period are signs of the instability and chaos our members are witnessing almost every day,” she said.

A spokesperson for MTC’s local subsidiary, Secure Journeys, said:

“In response to your questions, I can confirm that Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority.”

The Australian Border Force was contacted for comment.

australia.title: Mao’s Last Dancer Li Cunxin on his long-awaited follow-up: ‘I don’t think my publisher expected it to take 14 years!’
australia.snippet: As The Lucky Son picks up where Cunxin’s 2003 memoir left off, the renowned Chinese Australian ballet dancer reflects on sacrifices made ...
australia.content:
Some people live such extraordinary lives that a single autobiography simply won’t suffice. Li Cunxin has now written two. The renowned ballet dancer and former artistic director of Queensland Ballet had hoped he was finished writing his story after the phenomenal international success of his 2003 memoir, Mao’s Last Dancer. But life had other plans.

“Actually, I had signed a contract with Penguin Random House for a follow-up,” Cunxin says, from his home in Brisbane. “It was going to be about the lives of my brothers and friends in China, and the ways the country has changed over time. But then I was offered the job at Queensland Ballet and I had to dedicate all my time to that. I don’t think they were expecting [the sequel] to take 14 years!”

His second memoir, The Lucky Son, takes up precisely where Mao’s Last Dancer left off: as Cunxin and his ballet dancer wife Mary fly to their new lives at Houston Ballet under the directorship of Ben Stevenson. That outline of the proposed book on China can be glimpsed under the surface of this one, like a palimpsest; Cunxin’s six brothers’ lives are sketched, and a fascinating portrait of a country lifting itself from abject poverty to world superpower emerges.

“One of the things my mother taught me was to keep moving forward at all times,” Cunxin says. “Don’t think about the past, just concentrate on what is ahead.” That grit kept her children alive and was instrumental in shaping Cunxin’s dogged, highly ambitious personality.

Determination runs in the family. Mary was a deeply respected dancer herself, a career she sacrificed when she and Cunxin discovered their daughter Sophie was born profoundly deaf. “We were so fearful that Sophie would miss out on so much,” Cunxin says. “Music and dance and all the magical things.”

Mary immediately left the world of ballet (she would return years later as ballet mistress at Queensland Ballet) to teach Sophie to talk. “Mary was incredible,” Cunxin recalls. “She gave everything to the task.”

One one hand, it was a complete success. Sophie was fitted with a bionic ear (then known as a cochlear implant) and thrived; she embraced dance, had a successful education and excelled in the workplace. Cunxin and Mary assumed they’d done all that was needed.

But then in 2015, Sophie sent an email to her parents that shocked and devastated them. Sophie expressed frustration at her parents for wanting their daughter to hear; she felt she’d come halfway to meet their world, but they had not met hers. They had not even bothered to learn sign language. Her “deafness was her birthright”, Cunxin writes in the book. Now, he says, Sophie “is a kind of ambassador between the hearing and deaf communities”. And he and Mary have begun learning Auslan.

Cunxin’s dance career was so exemplary – moving from the Beijing Dance Academy to Houston Ballet, and then to principal artist at Australian Ballet – he could have been forgiven for hanging up his pointe shoes and walking into a lucrative position in a stockbroking firm. Indeed, that’s exactly what he did. An unsuccessful tilt at the artistic directorship of Australian Ballet (the role eventually went to David McAllister) utterly crushed him, and it seemed for a few years he would never return to the world of professional ballet.

Of course, that wasn’t how it panned out: despite being burned by that failure, Cunxin reluctantly put his name in the hat when Queensland Ballet were looking for their next artistic director. That tenacity and resolve was once more poured into the theatre.

“To be a leader of any kind takes vision,” Cunxin says. “I had a very strong vision for Queensland Ballet. But you also have to be a good communicator, because you need to inspire others to join in your vision.” And you need to apply yourself, which wasn’t such an issue for someone trained at Beijing Dance Academy, with its brutal rehearsal regime and exacting standards.

One of the delights of The Lucky Son is the way it tracks some of our favourite characters from Mao’s Last Dancer, including The Bandit, Cunxin’s bestie at the Beijing Dance Academy; his gorgeous instructor Teacher Xiao; and his astonishing mum and dad, Niang and Dia. There are echoes in the events too: Stevenson’s trip to Queensland to watch his protégé mount Cinderella recalls the unforgettable moment in Mao’s Last Dancer when his parents leave China for the first time to see their son dance and the audience gives them a standing ovation.

Central to Cunxin’s success at Queensland Ballet – where he oversaw a massive improvement in standards and built a stunning new home for the company, the Thomas Dixon Centre – were the lessons he learned from his time away from ballet, when he was a stockbroker: “I learned so much from the business world – when we had to approach donors for money, I could speak their language.” Relationships with Elisabeth Murdoch and the Ian Potter Foundation came in handy, and he and Mary also contributed some money of their own. It’s now a world-class organisation.

Looking back on his life now, Cunxin feels an overwhelming sense of “gratitude, for the opportunities I was given and the people and artists who shaped me”. The Lucky Son concludes on stage – hardly surprising, given so many of the key moments in Cunxin’s life have been there – but this time it is in Switzerland, where he was awarded ballet’s most prestigious award, the Prix de Lausanne, in 2025.

After a few years of serious health issues (Mary is a cancer survivor and Cunxin has a major heart condition), the couple are increasingly happy to chill. “Our health has forced us to slow down,” he says with the emphasis on forced, as if there were no way they would slow down on purpose. “I worked very hard for two years on this book – it’s been all-consuming. So yes, I am enjoying taking things a little slower.”

Is he confident that ballet will survive the coming AI tsunami, given how hard the art form is to perfect and how much time and effort is required? “I am worried, but I do think ballet is special,” he says. “When people come to see ballet, they are blown away by the artistry, the physicality and the music. I think it’s more important than ever to connect people.”

  • The Lucky Son by Li Cunxin is out now (Penguin, $36.99)

australia.title: Back to Back Barries: How Labor should fight One Nation – podcast
australia.snippet: Tony Barry and Jessie McCrone examine the latest Redbridge poll (‘the poll that stops the nation’) that shows a slump in support for the ...
australia.content:
Tony Barry and Jessie McCrone examine the latest Redbridge poll (‘the poll that stops the nation’) that shows a slump in support for the prime minister and weaker support for Labor.

Tony asks Jessie – a former senior Labor advisor – how she would counsel Anthony Albanese and what she thinks could improve Labor’s chances against Pauline Hanson’s One Nation.

The two former sparring partners also look at next month’s Victorian election and what it could mean for the major parties at a federal level.

Email the show: backtobackbarries@theguardian.com

  • One Nation celebrated stunning success in Queensland in 1998 – then it all fell apart. What happened?

australia.title: Seeing orange: Nationals under threat in regional Victoria as angry voters consider One Nation
australia.snippet: ‘No safe seats’ for Coalition partner at upcoming state election, Danny O’Brien says, amid fury about renewables, immigration and conditi...
australia.content:
On a Friday afternoon last month, Victorian Nationals leader Danny O’Brien was driving around his electorate putting up corflutes when he came across a herd of cows blocking a road near Poowong.

As he waited for them to pass, O’Brien began talking politics with the woman herding them.

He says she told him she “liked orange” – a reference to One Nation – and that it was “time to shake things up”. O’Brien replied that voting for the party could risk giving Labor a path to victory “through the middle”. She mulled it over, then chased after the cows.

That night, an email arrived from the woman offering to host one of O’Brien’s signs on the family paddock beside a busy road.

It’s these sorts of conversations, O’Brien says, that are crucial for his party in countering One Nation’s rise in regional Victoria.

The Nationals currently hold nine seats in the Victorian parliament’s lower house – having picked up three seats off independents at the 2022 election – its best result since 1943.

O’Brien credits the result to its candidate selection – he says the Victorian branch of the party have become skilled at identifying “local champions” with a preexisting profile and “attaching the Nationals brand” to them.

“It’s often been said we’re a loose collection of independents that share that passion for rural and regional Victoria,” he says. “It’s not necessarily about left or right.”

At this election, the party hopes to hold it’s exisiting seats while targeting Jacinta Allan’s former seat of Bendigo East – where they’ve preselected popular local pub owner Andrew Lethlean – as well as Labor-held Bendigo West and Ripon.

But recently, the political landscape has been upended. Polls show One Nation’s vote is hovering about 20% statewide – with support even higher in regional areas.

Victorian Labor’s internal polling leaked in June showed the Nationals could face a wipeout at November’s state election. Another poll, commissioned by Trades Hall, showed the Nationals losing at least three seats to Pauline Hanson’s party.

Federally, One Nation won its first lower house seat from the Coalition at the Farrer byelection and has continued to ascend, with the latest Guardian Essential poll showing its primary vote had climbed to 25%. This was ahead of the Liberal-National Coalition on it’s lowest-ever primary vote of 22% and not far behind Labor’s 29%.

“There are no safe seats and frankly, they haven’t been for a long time,” O’Brien says.

The Nationals MP for Mildura, Jade Benham, is more blunt: “One Nation are 100% our biggest threat.

“It’s not even about the candidate. The candidate is kind of inconsequential. It’s the brand now.”

‘People want to be able to stay here’

Cindy Madeley is the mayor of Wellington Shire, which overlaps with O’Brien’s electorate of Gippsland South. She says the region is in a “state of flux”, as industries its towns once relied on rapidly change.

She points to Sale, a town “that would not exist in the way it does without the oil and gas industry”, now watching Esso Australia decommission half its infrastructure hosted off the coast. In Yarram, a timber mill closed before Christmas, while others are importing Tasmanian timber as a consequence of Victoria’s native forest logging ban. There are plans for offshore wind, but it remains unclear how much the local community will benefit, she says.

“We’re worried about the things that everyone else is worried about – cost of living, interest rate rises, roads and hospitals – but when you add the regional lens to it, things become just that little bit harder,” Madeley says.

“People want to be able to stay here and for their kids to stay here. They just want things to get better.”

For Hanson, better means a return to a bygone era. Last month, she was in Morwell pledging to halt new transmission lines and renewable energy projects, keep Victoria’s largest coal plant operating and lift the ban on nuclear energy. Last week, the party also committed to bring back logging. It did not respond to a request to participate in this piece.

Guardian Australia didn’t spot any One Nation campaign material or evidence of a significant ground campaign during its visit to South Gippsland, with the exception of a seemingly AI-generated banner at Greenfield’s hotel on the Princes Highway in Traralgon, which featured a boxing kangaroo, Uluru and a smiling image of Hanson alongside the slogan “one flag, one voice”.

It was not clear who was responsible for the banner, which was illuminated by carefully placed lights, but one local resident spoke proudly of it, saying: “She has been taken down four times, but we keep putting her back up.”

Pearsondale cattle farmer Geoff Gooch says Hanson’s rhetoric has appealed to some of his friends.

“I’ve got a few friends that think she’s wonderful but they also listen to the Bolt Report – so there’s a direct correlation there,” Gooch says.

He says while Hanson might propose something that “sounds like a good idea”, her party’s policies aren’t practical. He says Australia cannot keep relying on coal and that “renewables are inevitable”, though the transition “has to be done sensibly”, while One Nation’s immigration plans would hurt the agricultural and dairy industries that rely on seasonal workers.

“If people vote for them, they’re not looking at the bigger picture,” Gooch says.

But for Con, a retiree who would not provide his surname and who migrated to Australia as a 10-pound pom and worked on major infrastructure projects including the high court of Australia, the West Gate Bridge and the Snowy Mountains scheme, One Nation’s immigration rhetoric resonates, even though he remains undecided on who to vote for in November.

“If I buy a farm to accommodate 500 cattle, I don’t go buying 1,000 of them,” he says.

Con, speaking to the Guardian at a bus stop in Sale, says while he didn’t believe Hanson in the 1990s, “everything she was saying then has come true”.

‘It feels like a civil war regarding renewables’

Annabelle Cleeland is the Nationals MP for Euroa in Victoria’s north-east. She shot to prominence during January’s devastating bushfires, leading her community’s response as her own family lost 1,000 livestock.

She says people in the electorate remain “deeply angry” – and that it extends beyond the bushfires to a growing divide between the quality of life in Melbourne and regional Victoria.

“I know of people who have called for an ambulance and they never turned up … we can’t get a podiatrist, we can’t get a speech therapist, we can’t give birth in our communities. We have no protection through a disaster,” she says.

With Victoria’s deteriorating road system shaping up to be one of the defining issues of the upcoming election, Cleeland says the Nationals have “been banging on about potholes years before it became a hot topic”.

“In regional Victoria, we know the individuals that have had accidents and we know the lives that we’ve lost in our community because of the condition of the roads,” she says.

Then there’s the government’s fast-tracked renewable energy approvals and controversial laws that allow state body VicGrid and its contractors access to private land – without a landholder’s consent.

“In parts of the state it feels like a civil war regarding renewables,” Cleeland says.

But she says the answer to that anger is “not a protest vote, but voting in an alternative government” – a message opposition leader, Jess Wilson, has repeated in recent weeks.

O’Brien says it was this point that got the Poowong farmer on board.

“If you want change then you’ve got to support us,” he says.

Benham used M&Ms to demonstrate a similar message. She shared a video on social media last month warning that a split in the “conservative vote” could make it harder for the Coalition to win the 16 seats it needs to form government, potentially handing Labor a fourth term she says would be “catastrophic”.

“There’s been a lot of people that are angry that I took out all the orange ones, but there’s been more people that are saying this is such a simple, easy way to understand it,” she says.

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist turned pollster with Redbridge, earlier this year described the Victorian Nationals brand as the “strongest in the country”. He maintains the party is “well-poised to defend themselves” against One Nation.

“They are demonstrating if people want change – but not chaos – they are the ones to deliver it,” he says.

“It won’t convert every One Nation supporter but it’s potentially enough to allow the Coalition to win those three-way contests.”

australia.title: As federal politicians vow to cut immigration, regional Queensland businesses need ‘every hand we can get’
australia.snippet: International working holidaymakers make up over 60% of the staff in some regional hospitality companies Get our breaking news email , fr...
australia.content:
A working holiday visa changed Sydney Schetter’s life.

The barista came to Australia from a small town outside Edmonton in Alberta in 2019. When she returns to Canada after her visa runs out next month, she won’t be alone.

“My partner, who’s Australian, is probably going to come next year when his visa gets approved,” she says.

During that seven-year stretch, Schetter was able to travel around Australia and abroad, learn a trade and make friends from around the world.

That was only possible because she lived in regional Queensland during the Covid-19 restrictions. Her nominally one-year visa was repeatedly extended due to her work at the Watermark hotel on Townsville’s Strand waterfront, and thanks to loosening of visa rules early in the pandemic.

Schetter says she’d never have done any of that if the federal Labor government’s new rules had been in place.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, announced last month that the government would cap the number of second-year working visa holders at 45,000, down from 57,000, and third year at just 5,000, less than one-sixth the approximately 31,000 issued currently.

Applicants will enter a ballot to be one of the lucky few. Holidaymakers from the United Kingdom will be exempt, as they already are from regional work.

“I wouldn’t even bother applying for my second year, maybe,” Schetter says.

That wouldn’t just crimp working holidaymakers’ love lives, it might also harm the economy. North Queensland’s business community says they are so dependent on workers like Schetter they’re concerned that if short-term visa holders like her do choose to stay away it could mean insolvency.

Australia has been issuing one-year working holiday visas since the Whitlam government. John Howard added a second year in 2005, on condition the worker do at least 88 days’ work in a prescribed industry in regional Australia, a category that defined so broadly it includes the Gold Coast, Newcastle and the entire states of Tasmania and South Australia plus the Northern Territory. There’s been a third year available since 2019.

Businesses worry the reform will reduce the value of the 88-day rule, meaning workers may choose Sydney or Melbourne over Townsville.

That would have a real impact on worker numbers. According to a recent survey by the Townsville chamber of commerce, about 70% of local businesses employed at least 10 working holiday visa holders, well over 60% of their total staff headcount.

Bart Furst, a director of Kickon Group, which owns the Watermark hotel, says they can employ upwards of 40 or 60 people on a working holiday visa, out of a total of 120 staff. Townsville has a low unemployment rate and Furst says he can’t convince locals to work there.

“A lot of [working holiday visa makers] have said they’d look at New Zealand or something before even visiting here,” he says.

He says they could be forced to cut back hours, as many businesses did when backpacker labour dried up early in the pandemic.

‘What’s the argument for changing this’?

The business backlash has spilled over into local politics.

The Queensland premier, David Crisafulli, who grew up in Ingham and often reminds the state his family are Italian migrants who worked the region’s cane fields, has repeatedly called the policy “nuts”.

Townsville LNP MP Adam Baillie says working holiday visa holders are “central to our economy here in north Queensland”.

“In regional Queensland, we need every hand we can get.”

In Cairns, even the Labor MP is unhappy. There are an estimated 5,500 working holiday visa holders in the popular backpacker destination, according to the local chamber of commerce.

State MP Michael Healy, a former hotelier and current shadow minister for tourism, says since last month’s immigration reduction announcement he has received angry calls from everyone from publicans in the Atherton Tablelands to Great Barrier Reef tourism operators.

“We need migration, and we need backpackers, particularly in regional Queensland and regional Australia,” he says.

Healy says the policy would slow the growth of Cairns. It could even knock the city into recession.

“What is the argument to changing this? What is the science behind that?”

Federal Labor MP for Leichhardt and Cairns local, Matt Smith, will lead a delegation of local business leaders to Canberra to meet Burke. Smith says his role is “making sure the far north’s voice is being heard” – but isn’t against the policy. They aren’t asking for a reversal of course.

“The thing that no one has objected to was that the numbers have been unsustainable,” he says.

“Everyone acknowledges that it’s now about refining the process so that the workforce is going where the workforce needs to be, and it needs to be in the far north.”

Announcing the changes, Burke said his immigration policy would slash net overseas migration (Nom) to about 225,000 in 2027-28, down from 292,000, and would “ensure that our migration system can be better targeted to the current needs of Australia”.

The Coalition responded with an even higher cut to migration, reducing the figure to 100,000 for the first two years from 2028-29.
The Nom target would then rise to 130,000 in the third year and 160,000 in 2031-32.

One Nation is aiming for zero net migration. After three years [when their policies would mean net negative Nom], One Nation said it would set a Nom “ceiling” of 130,000 a year.

‘We’ve got no young people’

Working holidaymakers represent Australia’s second-largest source of immigration. About 78,300 arrived in the country in 2024–25, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, compared with 146,700 university students. There were about 206,000 working holidaymakers the country at last count.

It has been estimated that every 100 visas create about five net full-time equivalent jobs in Australia. Most backpackers live in the big cities, but more than half the jobs they work are in two industries: tourism and agriculture.

Kaya Barry, senior lecturer at Griffith University, says the government could have targeted student visas rather than working holidays to slash net migration, but didn’t want to deal with the political consequences of hitting the university sector, she says.

“It’s a divide between metro and regional Australia, and I think that’s an easy [choice],” she says.

“The votes are not in regional Australia. People in cities don’t know what backpackers do beyond them partying at Bondi.”

There are working holiday visas across regional Australia, she says, working as au pairs, fencers or nurses.

The impact of losing young people will go beyond the economic, particularly in small-town Australia, she says. Barry travelled across the country in 2022 studying the visa class, just after the border opened. Without working holidaymakers, many towns were struggling, they’d lost vibrancy, she says.

“They were like, ‘We’ve got no young people. The pub had to close, didn’t have enough business,’” she says.

“You’ve got 49 nations who come into a regional town. The cultural immersion that the individuals get on the visa, but also the hosting communities in farming areas or tourism areas, it can’t be understated”.

Schetter says she’ll be sad to turn her back on Australia next month. At least part of the decision is, once again, about visas.

It’d be much harder for her to get permanent residency in Australia – a place she has lived in for seven years – than it will be for her partner, Sam, to move to Canada, even though he has never been there. It’ll also be much cheaper.

“The partner visa for him to come to Canada is less than $3,000. Anyone that I know who’s done partner visas paid more than $10,000, including the lawyer,” she says.

world.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
world.snippet: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza Nobel peace pri...
world.content:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.

Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.

“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded in disbelief.

“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”

Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.

In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Donald Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.

On Monday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

world.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
world.snippet: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the f...
world.content:
Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.

The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.

In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.

Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.

The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.

In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

world.title: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues
world.snippet: Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood Egyptian journalists...
world.content:
Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.

Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.

One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.

“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.

In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.

Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.

Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Journalists’ Syndicate, whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.

Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.

The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.

For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.

“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

world.title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island
world.snippet: Free-roaming Aldabra population far exceeds human population of Seychelles after decades-long recovery programme A survey of the world’s ...
world.content:
A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving.

A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.

The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island. This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.

The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.

Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.

Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”

Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.

The study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.

“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.

“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.

“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”

world.title: Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray
world.snippet: Government forces’ attack raises risk of internal conflict in Ethiopia that could trigger regional war Eritrean troops who crossed into E...
world.content:
Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries.

Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled.

Eritrean troops were then targeted by Ethiopian government drones on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, Acled said.

Eritrea has a historical enmity with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an offensive against the Ethiopian government on 23 September, but that previous hostility has been superseded by Eritrea’s desire to head off a perceived risk of Ethiopia invading it, in order to access the Red Sea.

In the last two weeks, the TPLF and six other armed groups in Ethiopia have fought the government in Tigray and the neighbouring regions Amhara and Afar. Ethiopia’s military pushed back and an allied militia, the Tigray Peace Force, took over Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 4 October after the TPLF withdrew from the city.

Eritrea’s information minister, Yemane Ghebremeskel, said in a statement: “We are not in the business of refuting wild allegations or narratives.” He did not explicitly confirm or deny the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia.

Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Monday: “Ethiopia stands ready to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and core national interests, while urging all regional actors to address shared challenges through constructive dialogue, partnership, and adherence to the principles of good neighbourliness rather than confrontation and zero-sum approaches.”

The TPLF and Ethiopia’s government fought a brutal civil war from 2020 to 2022. Between 300,000 and 800,000 civilians died, according to British government estimates. Both sides and their allies were accused of war crimes.

Eritrea intervened on the side of Ethiopia in that conflict, after a rapprochement between the two countries in 2018, which earned Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, the 2019 Nobel peace prize.

Eritrea, which gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, has a long enmity with the TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018. The two countries fought a war from 1998 to 2000.

Relations between the countries have deteriorated again in recent years. Abiy has said Ethiopia needs access to the Red Sea, and state media has claimed the country has historical rights to the Eritrean port of Assab. The US-Israeli war on Iran – leading Iran to limit shipping through the strait of Hormuz – has further raised the stakes of Red Sea access.

In its statement on Monday, Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said: “Any serious discussion of regional maritime affairs and security architecture must account for Ethiopia’s legitimate interests and its enduring connection to the Red Sea.”

Yemane said in a post on X on Wednesday that Ethiopia was “incessantly beating the drums of war and openly stating … that it will launch a war of aggression against Eritrea to acquire what it calls ‘sovereign access to the sea’ … In recent weeks, it has tried to repackage this war agenda in terms of ‘self-defence’ by fabricating various allegations against Eritrea.”

Magnus Taylor, Horn of Africa deputy director at the Crisis Group thinktank, said: “The big worry is that [Abiy] might try to solve all his problems at the same time, by invading Eritrea, possibly a regime change move and also a land grab for the Red Sea port, and also solving his problem with Tigray at the same time. It’s a very ambitious military agenda, though.”

While the full impact of the fighting on Tigrayan civilians is not clear, reports have emerged of the TPLF forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15 to fight.

“The civilians in these three regions [Tigray, Amhara and Afar] didn’t get healed from the first round of violence that was halted by the peace agreement [in 2022],” said Acled Ethiopia analyst Jalale Getachew Birru. “They just started healing recently.”
